description_full: Meta Platforms, Inc. engages in the development of products that enable people to connect and share with friends and family through mobile devices, personal computers, virtual reality (VR) headsets, and AI glasses in the United States, Canada, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and internationally. It operates through two segments, Family of Apps (FoA) and Reality Labs (RL). The FoA segment offers Facebook, which enables people to build community through feed, reels, stories, groups, marketplace, and other; Instagram that brings people closer through Instagram feed, stories, reels, live, and messaging; Messenger, a messaging application for people to connect with friends, family, communities, and businesses across platforms and devices through text, audio, and video calls; Meta AI, an assistant that's available across apps, as a stand-alone app, on AI glasses, and on the web; Threads, an application for text-based updates and public conversations; and WhatsApp, a messaging application that is used by people and businesses to communicate and transact. The RL segment provides virtual and augmented reality products, including consumer hardware, software, and content that help people feel connected, as well as Meta Quest devices that enable social experiences across gaming, fitness, entertainment, and more. The segment also includes wearables such as AI glasses like Ray Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses; and the Meta Ray Ban Display, which combines AI glasses with an integrated lens display and the Meta Neural Band, a wrist worn device using electromyography that lets people control their AI glasses through neuromuscular signals. Meta Platforms, Inc. has a collaboration with Microsoft Corporation, NVIDIA Corporation, Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., Broadcom Inc., and OpenAI, L.L.C. The company was formerly known as Facebook, Inc. and changed its name to Meta Platforms, Inc. in October 2021. The company was incorporated in 2004 and is headquartered in Menlo Park, California.

financial_summary: Meta Platforms, Inc. is a mega-cap communication services business with a $1.6T market cap on $201.0B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +20% over the past three years and +27% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +2.4pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 38% against a 11% cost of capital — a 28-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $46.1B in free cash flow — roughly 23 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.92× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 71× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.9%, a thin return of capital, and stock-based comp at 10% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 41% operating margin runs 33pp above the Communication Services median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.02x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 8.3% of sector revenue and 16.9% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 171 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 25% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 42% and a beta of 1.26, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.09 vs 5y 1.39), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $11.8B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash and 74% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $641 (margin of safety -0%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 11%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $383 to $1,093 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: P/E 21.9 vs 15.4, EV/EBITDA 14.0 vs 9.9 and P/FCF 35.6 vs 11.1 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-7%).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 57 covering analysts target $850 on average, 32% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 38% clears the cost of capital of 10.5% by 28pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.41).
It converts 23% of revenue into free cash flow, or 13% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 1.92x, but a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
ROE of 28% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 28.5% of revenue on R&D and 10.2% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $22.8B (1% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 19.9% over 3 years, 18.5% over 5 years and 27.3% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
At current returns, reinvesting 88% of profits supports about 30.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.3% a year over five years.
Capex runs 3.7x depreciation (34.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 78%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (62 sales, net $85.0M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.9% (1.6% in buybacks and 0.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 66,775 employees, each generates about $3.0M of revenue, 4.9x the Communication Services median, and revenue has grown 32.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $691K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $25.1M (8x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
